clue.text: With one drink entering exams in wickedness that's passed on

indicators.note: entering tells us the one-plus-drink pair goes inside the word for exams

parts.note: orals are spoken examinations
I is the Roman numeral for one
gin is a spirit, a drink
taken as written

explanation.surface: A drinker turns up tipsy to their exams, a moral failing that runs in the family.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With' is only a link; 'entering' places the one-and-drink pair inside the exams word, and the final 'in' is used as printed.
explanation.definitionFit: The theological doctrine holds that humanity inherits a sinful state from Adam, so it is wickedness handed down.

clue.text: Guardian's letter from Europe outwardly left Freudian slip — that's novel

parts.note: the newspaper speaking of itself would say 'our'
mu is a letter of the Greek alphabet, Greece being in Europe

indicators.note: a slip is a mistake, so the letters are jumbled up
outwardly means only the outer letters of the word left are used

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A Guardian writer makes a Freudian slip in a letter from Europe, and remarks how novel it is.
explanation.walkthrough: Freudian slip looks like one phrase, but 'slip' alone is the anagram signal: LT (outside letters of 'left') with FREUDIAN gives TUALFRIEND. OUR MUTUAL FRIEND is Dickens's last completed novel.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the title of the final completed novel by Charles Dickens, published 1864-65.

clue.text: Arab republicans have quite intelligent leaders

parts.note: the IRA is the Irish Republican Army, militant republicans

indicators.note: the leaders of the words are their first letters

explanation.surface: A claim that Arab republicans are led by fairly bright people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Have' is a link word joining the two parts.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone from Iraq is an Arab national, so the demonym serves as an example of an Arab.

clue.text: Compiler shall bequeath malevolence

parts.note: the setter speaking of himself would say 'I'll', I shall
to bequeath something is to will it to someone

explanation.surface: The setter announces that he will leave nothing but spite in his testament.
explanation.walkthrough: Crosswords often use 'compiler' or 'setter' for I or ME; here 'Compiler shall' is the contraction I'LL.
explanation.definitionFit: Bad feeling or hostility towards someone is a direct synonym of malevolence.

clue.text: Rain falls? Yes, it regularly makes us shrink

indicators.note: regularly means taking every other letter of the run Rain falls yes it

explanation.surface: A gloomy rainy day is enough to make anyone feel smaller.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shrink' looks like a verb describing what rain does, but it is the slang noun for a psychiatrist; 'makes us' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Shrink is informal slang for a psychiatrist or psychoanalyst, a professional who analyses minds.

clue.text: Unorthodox priest admits two partners and one who hasn't a partner

indicators.note: admits means one part lets another inside it
unorthodox means not in the usual form, so the letters of priest are rearranged

parts.note: N and S, North and South, are partners at the bridge table

explanation.surface: A rule-breaking priest takes in a couple and an unmarried person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'admits' puts NS inside SPITER, an anagram of PRIEST. In bridge, North and South play as partners, a regular crossword convention.
explanation.definitionFit: An unmarried woman, traditionally one past usual marrying age, is someone without a spouse.

clue.text: Perhaps major politician with large troops — it's bad and mad

parts.note: a major is a commissioned officer, so is 'no NCO' (non-commissioned officer)
MP, Member of Parliament, is a politician
OS, outsize, is a clothing abbreviation for large
men are soldiers, troops

indicators.note: bad signals the letters of it's going wrong, being rearranged

explanation.surface: A ranting army officer turned politician leading his troops is judged deranged.
explanation.walkthrough: The neat trick is that a major is NO NCO, as majors hold commissions; 'bad' turns IT'S into TIS. 'with' and 'and' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin legal phrase means 'not in control of the mind', i.e. insane.

clue.text: Travel document for Paris? Assez, les bêtises!

indicators.note: French for blunders or nonsense, signalling the preceding letters are messed up

explanation.surface: A French official, exasperated, cries 'enough of this nonsense!' over a permit for Paris.
explanation.walkthrough: The French indicator suits the French answer: 'Assez, les bêtises!' means 'Enough nonsense!'. A laissez-passer is a pass permitting free travel.
explanation.definitionFit: This French term names a permit or pass allowing the holder to travel through a territory.

clue.text: Snog (with intent) had perhaps led to this?

definitions.text: Snog (with intent) had perhaps led to this?

indicators.note: perhaps led to suggests the words before were reshaped into something else

explanation.surface: A kiss with intent may well have ended in a brief fling.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition and the wordplay at once: the letters of SNOG INTENT HAD rearrange to the result such a kiss might lead to.
explanation.definitionFit: A single sexual encounter with no ongoing relationship is what an intentional snog could end in.

clue.text: Top familiar arrangement of surface letters? No!

indicators.note: an arrangement means the letters are reordered
to top something is to cut off its head, so the first letter of familiar goes

parts.note: taken as written before its head is removed

explanation.surface: Someone scoffs at the idea that their well-known letters come by surface mail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Top' as a verb beheads FAMILIAR to AMILIAR, which is then rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Post carried by aeroplane is contrasted with surface mail, the slow route by land or sea.

clue.text: Bridgetown has crazy paving stones with steps somehow missing

indicators.note: crazy paving, with its random stones, signals the letters are jumbled
somehow missing says the letters of steps, in any order, are taken away

explanation.surface: A town known for its bridge has haphazard paving where the steps have disappeared.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove S, T, E, P, S from PAVING STONES and rearrange the rest. Avignon in France is famed for its bridge in the song 'Sur le pont d'Avignon'.
explanation.definitionFit: The French city is renowned for its medieval bridge, the Pont Saint-Bénézet, so it is a town of the bridge.

clue.text: Saint ousts leader for greed and lack of intelligence

indicators.note: ousts leader means the first letter is pushed out and replaced

parts.note: cupidity means greed for wealth

explanation.surface: A holy man rejects avarice and dimwittedness.
explanation.definitionFit: Being slow-witted or foolish is exactly a want of intelligence.

clue.text: Disdain for 20 at last changing direction

indicators.note: the final letter, a compass point, swaps for another compass point

parts.note: a score is twenty

explanation.surface: Someone looks down on twenty for changing course at the end.
explanation.walkthrough: '20' looks like a cross-reference to 20-across but is simply the number. E (east) becomes N (north).
explanation.definitionFit: Contempt or open disdain for someone is a close synonym.

clue.text: Australians implicated in the return of consumerism

indicators.note: return means the run is read backwards
implicated in signals a run of letters held within the word

explanation.surface: Australians are blamed for the comeback of consumer culture.
explanation.walkthrough: The run SUME sits inside 'consumerism' and is read backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: These large flightless birds are native to Australia, so they are Australians in a whimsical sense.

clue.text: He is to begin proceedings, say, after idiot found on line

indicators.note: after places the following pieces behind the idiot

parts.note: a clot is a fool
he's is the contraction of he is

indicators.note: to begin means only the first letter of proceedings

parts.note: e.g. means for example, say

explanation.surface: A man is set to open a trial, apparently, after a fool turns up on the phone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'found on line' looks like a phone call but refers to a washing line.
explanation.definitionFit: A clip for fixing wet laundry is a thing seen on a washing line.

clue.text: Clever ones get E's

parts.note: the heads of the word egg, its first letters, are E's

explanation.surface: Bright pupils score E grades.
explanation.walkthrough: An E grade is poor, so the surface is a paradox; the clue reads 'egg heads' as the first letters of EGG.
explanation.definitionFit: Intellectuals or highbrow people are informally called this, often a little mockingly.

clue.text: The other place might be cool

indicators.note: other means the letters take another form, rearranged

explanation.surface: Hell, the other place, might turn out to be chilly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The other place' looks like a euphemism for hell, but 'other' is the anagram signal on PLACE MIGHT.
explanation.definitionFit: A calm, unexcitable temperament is cool-headed.

clue.text: What's to be done with another order of magnitude, when it's gone

indicators.note: another order means the letters are put in a new sequence
gone says the letters of it are removed

explanation.surface: A task becomes an order of magnitude bigger once it has gone.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove I and T from MAGNITUDE and rearrange MAGNUDE.
explanation.definitionFit: This Latin gerundive, singular of the plural list word, literally means a thing that must be done.

clue.text: Conclude with rejection of the afterlife, perhaps

parts.note: to infer is to conclude from evidence
no is a refusal

explanation.surface: Someone decides the afterlife can be dismissed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with' is a link; 'perhaps' signals the definition is one example of an afterlife.
explanation.definitionFit: Hell, as depicted by Dante, is one version of what awaits after death.

clue.text: I forgot to mention at the start, so try and pay attention!

parts.note: PS, postscript, adds what the writer forgot to mention

indicators.note: at the start means the first letters of so and try

explanation.surface: An afterthought, then a plea to listen.
explanation.definitionFit: This hissed interjection is used to attract someone's attention discreetly.

clue.text: Heartless Harry's knocked back wine

indicators.note: knocked back means the letters are read backwards, like a drink downed
heartless means the central letter of the name is removed

parts.note: Harry's is read as Harry plus the S of 'is'

explanation.surface: Unfeeling Harry has downed his glass of red.
explanation.walkthrough: HARRYS loses its middle R to make HARYS, which reads backwards. 'Knocked back' doubles as drinking slang.
explanation.definitionFit: This red grape variety, also called Shiraz, names the wine made from it.

clue.text: Heard F here in 10, half decent and streamlined

parts.note: the letter F said aloud is spelt eff
10 is Avignon, in France, where 'here' is ici

indicators.note: half takes the back half of decent

explanation.surface: In a French town a musician hears a note in a well-ordered performance.
explanation.walkthrough: '10' refers to 10-across, AVIGNON: French for 'here' is ICI. The rear half of 'decent' is ENT.
explanation.definitionFit: Something streamlined has been made to work with no waste, which is the sense here.

clue.text: Message for the business secretary?

definitions.meaning: a telegram is a message sent by wire
Vince ... was UK Business Secretary from 2010 to 2015

explanation.walkthrough: When this ran in 2012 Vince Cable was Britain's Secretary of State for Business; the question mark flags the name.
explanation.definitionFit: A telegram sent by wire is called this, and the surname belongs to the then minister.

clue.text: Dodgy dealer accepts milestone

indicators.note: accepts means one part takes another inside it
dodgy means unreliable, so the letters of dealer are shifted around

explanation.surface: A shady trader takes in a roadside marker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'milestone' must be split into 'mile' (M) and 'stone', the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: This green beryl is a precious gem, a stone.

clue.text: To add insult to injury, take part in destruction

indicators.note: in places the part inside the word for destruction

parts.note: ruin means destruction
a bit is a part

explanation.surface: A vandal is urged to join in the wrecking.
explanation.definitionFit: To keep emphasising someone's mistake makes them feel worse, idiomatically.

clue.text: Sides with Marxist leader below ground — shows guts

indicators.note: ground means crushed, so the letters are broken up and remade
leader means the first letter of Marxist

explanation.surface: A politician joins the Marxist leader underground, showing courage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shows guts' suggests bravery but means removing entrails; 'ground' is the anagram signal, not 'below ground'.
explanation.definitionFit: To remove an animal's intestines is to expose its innards, literally showing them.
